title: Called by name (Isaiah 43:1–3)
hook: fear not, I have called you by name; when you pass through the waters

segments.voice: Yesterday, a promise for the tired, and your line was wings like eagles. Did you rest before you ran? Day four hundred sixty-nine.

A crowded airport. Hundreds of people, announcements in three languages, nobody looking at anybody. Then, over the noise, someone calls out your name. Not "excuse me." Not "sir" or "ma'am." Your name. And you turn, instantly, before you've even thought about it. There's something in a name that cuts through everything. The exiles in Babylon were a small, defeated people inside the biggest city of their world, easy to lose in the crowd. They felt unseen, overlooked, swallowed. Isaiah has comforted them and promised them strength. Now he says something even more personal. Today, the name.
screen: `A CROWDED AIRPORT.` → `SOMEONE CALLS YOUR NAME.` → `EXILES, LOST IN THE CROWD.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "But now thus saith the LORD that created thee, O Jacob, and he that formed thee, O Israel, Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine." Notice the verbs. Created, formed. Formed is a potter's word, the same one used when God shapes the first human from the dust in Genesis. Then redeemed: the word for a family member who buys back a relative sold into debt, or buys back the family land. Then called by name. Then the three words of today's carry: thou art mine. Not a possession, the way you own a phone. Belonging, the way a child belongs to a family. And then the promise, with water and fire: "When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned." It doesn't say you'll never pass through the waters. It says when. The flood and the fire are assumed. What's promised is company in them, and that they won't sweep you away. These words were first spoken to a whole people, Jacob and Israel, and Jewish readers hear them that way. Christians have also heard them personally for centuries, and many churches read them at baptisms, where someone is named and passes through the water. This week in the prophets: here am I, swords into plowshares, unto us a child, the wolf and the lamb, comfort ye, wings like eagles, and today, called by name. A week that moved from a prophet saying send me to God saying you are mine.
screen: `CREATED, FORMED, REDEEMED.` · `CALLED BY NAME: THOU ART MINE.` · `NOT IF, BUT WHEN.` · `A PEOPLE, AND EACH PERSON.` · then, large: `I HAVE CALLED THEE BY THY NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say your name as if God said it. Settle, and breathe. Say your own name silently, the one people who love you use. Notice how it feels: maybe tender, maybe awkward, maybe heavy with what other people have said in that tone. Now say it again, slowly, as if it were spoken by someone who made you and isn't disappointed. Then let the next words follow: fear not. Let them rest on whatever you're passing through right now. If you pray, you can simply listen. The bell holds the time.
Called by name. God's word to the exiles in Isaiah forty-three: created, formed, redeemed, and named. Fear not; you are mine.
Your line: you are mine. Today, use people's names on purpose: the cashier, the coworker, the neighbor. Let someone feel seen in the crowd. Day four hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Isaiah 43:1–3 is often read at Christian baptisms and confirmations, and many Christians turn to it in times of fear or illness; it is also set in hymns and songs used in worship.

original.note: Hebrew: I have called you by your name; you are mine.

trapdoor: what you thought: a comforting verse that nothing bad will happen.
what it means: God names a frightened people as his own and promises to be with them in the flood and the fire.
what a scholar hears: four verbs in a row, created, formed, redeemed, called. formed (yatsar) is the potter's verb of Genesis 2:7; redeemed (ga'al) is the kinsman's duty.
